title: Inheritance: Reuse a Class Without Copying It
excerpt: Build a new class on top of an existing one, override methods, call the parent with super(), and check types with isinstance.

headings.text: A Parent Class and a Child Class

html:
You have a Dog class with a name and a way to describe itself. Now you need a Cat class, and it needs the same name and the same way to describe itself. Copying the code across works until you fix a bug in one copy and forget the other.

Inheritance lets a new class start with everything an existing class has, and then add or change only what is different. The existing class is called the parent (or base class), and the new one is the child (or subclass).

Some terms first: a class is a blueprint for objects, __init__ stores an object's starting data, and self is the object a method is working on.

The Copy-Paste Problem

Here are two animal classes written the obvious way, by copying:

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name} is an animal"

class Cat:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name} is an animal"

print(Dog("Rex").describe())
print(Cat("Tom").describe())
Rex is an animal
Tom is an animal

The two classes are identical in everything except their names. If you later change how describe works, you must remember to change it twice, and with ten animal classes that gets out of hand.

A Parent Class and a Child Class

Move the shared code into one parent class, then name it in parentheses when you define the child (the word pass means "nothing more to add"):

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name} is an animal"

    def speak(self):
        return "..."

class Dog(Animal):
    pass

rex = Dog("Rex")

print(rex.describe())
print(rex.speak())
Rex is an animal
...

The child class Dog contains nothing of its own, yet rex can describe itself and speak. It inherited both methods, and the __init__ as well, from Animal. Fix a bug in the parent and every child benefits.

Override What Is Different

The inherited speak returns a placeholder. What if the child wants a different answer? A child can override a method by defining one with the same name, and Python will use the child's version:

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "Woof"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "Meow"

print(Dog("Rex").speak())
print(Cat("Tom").speak())
print(Animal("Generic").speak())
Woof
Meow
...

Each class answers in its own way, while describe is still shared. The parent itself is unchanged. (The dots returned by the parent's speak are just placeholder text.)

Extend the Parent With super()

What if the child needs extra data, such as a dog's breed? You can write the child's own __init__, but you do not want to repeat the parent's setup. The function super() reaches the parent class, so the child can reuse its __init__ and then add more:

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.breed = breed

    def speak(self):
        return "Woof"

rex = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")

print(rex.name, rex.breed)
print(rex.describe())
Rex Labrador
Rex is an animal

The call super().__init__(name) ran the parent's setup, which stored the name, and then the child stored the breed.

Checking Types

Because a Dog is a kind of Animal, Python knows it. Is a Dog also an Animal as far as Python is concerned? Yes. isinstance() asks whether an object belongs to a class, including its parent classes, and issubclass() asks the same about classes:

print(isinstance(rex, Dog))
print(isinstance(rex, Animal))
print(issubclass(Dog, Animal))
print(isinstance(rex, Cat))
True
True
True
False

You can also ask Python in which order it searches for a method. It looks in the object's own class first, then in the parent, and so on up the chain. Every class quietly inherits from a built-in class called object, which is why it appears last:

print(Dog.__mro__)
(<class '__main__.Dog'>, <class '__main__.Animal'>, <class 'object'>)

One Call, Many Behaviors

The real payoff comes when you handle different kinds of animals in one loop, without checking what each one is. Do you need an if for every type? No: each object already knows how to speak in its own way.

pets = [Dog("Rex", "Labrador"), Cat("Tom")]

for pet in pets:
    print(pet.name, "says", pet.speak())
Rex says Woof
Tom says Meow

When Not to Use Inheritance

A good test is the sentence "a Dog is a kind of Animal". If that sounds natural, inheritance fits. If the relationship is really "has a", such as a Car that has an Engine, store one object inside the other as an attribute instead. Inheritance is a strong tool; use it only when the "is a" sentence is true.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonInheritance.ipynb.

Summary

  • class Child(Parent): makes a child class that inherits all attributes and methods of the parent.
  • A child can override an inherited method by defining one with the same name.
  • super().__init__(...) runs the parent's setup so the child can add its own data on top.
  • isinstance(obj, Class) is true for the object's own class and every parent class.
  • Python searches the object's class first, then the parent classes in order.
  • Use inheritance when the relationship reads as "is a"; use an attribute when it reads as "has a".
